items.text: Products: structures and accessibility
A structure given by products up to $\pi$: a functor $\mathbf{Sets}\to\mathbf{Sets}$ with extra structure, commuting with $\pi$-filtering direct limits.
With arbitrary products the condition can be dropped, or replaced: each operation factors through a sub-sum of bounded cardinality (a small set of operations).
Accessibility: both adjoint functors between accessible categories (e.g. $S$ and $\mathbf{Sets}$) are accessible.
Birkhoff's theorem
$S$ defined by products; $S'\subset S$ stable under products, subobjects, quotients. Then $S'$ is defined by equations: adding axioms (arrows made equal).
The inclusion $S'\hookrightarrow S$ has an adjoint: take all quotients of $X$ lying in $S'$ and form their inverse limit.
Standard counterexample to the converse direction:
S=\mathbf{Ab},\qquad S'=\text{torsion-free abelian groups}\ \ (\text{full, not definable by equations})
S'\subset S\ \longleftrightarrow\ R\to R'\ \ \text{bijective on objects, surjective on arrows;}\ \ R'=R/(\text{equations})
A small set of equations? Birkhoff's original: finite products; here products up to $\pi$.
Making an arrow invertible is not stable under subobjects or quotients.
Full subcategories with left adjoint: many more than the Birkhoff ones. Birkhoff singles out those corresponding to equalising arrows.
\text{full } S'\hookrightarrow S \text{ over the same base objects, with left adjoint, } S'\to\mathbf{Sets}^I \text{ tripleable}
Conjectured criterion: the inclusion admits a left adjoint and the composite to sets is tripleable (perhaps the adjoint is automatic).
\mathbf{Gp}\subset\mathbf{Mon}:\quad \mathbb N\subset\mathbb Z\ \text{is a submonoid of a group that is not a group}
So groups are not definable among monoids by equations: not stable under subobjects. (Existence of inverses, not equations.)
Birkhoff selects exactly the subcategories with a left adjoint and tripleable composite — and more restrictive than that.
Pseudo-topoi
$\Delta$ = pseudo-topoi: Giraud's axioms (a, b, c); functors commuting with arbitrary direct limits and finite inverse limits.
a) some limits: arbitrary direct limits, finite inverse limits;
b) sums disjoint and universal;
c) equivalence relations effective, universally.
The functors are inverse images $f^*$: morphisms of topoi go the other way.
T\colon\Delta\to\mathbf{Cat},\qquad f\colon F\to E\ \Longrightarrow\ f^*\colon T(E)\to T(F)
Example: a group in $E$ has an inverse image under $F\to E$.
Classifying topos: a universal structure in $T(E)$ such that for every topos $F$:
T(F)\ \simeq\ \underline{\operatorname{Top}}(F,E)^{\circ},\qquad f\ \mapsto\ f^*(\xi)
Contravariant in $f$: « 2-corepresentable » rather than 2-representable.
Problem 1: the enveloping topos
$C$ a small category: the enveloping (pseudo-)topos exists. First case: $C$ has finite inverse limits (a type of structure described by finite inverse limits).
\Delta(C)=\widehat C=\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(C^\circ,\mathbf{Sets}),\qquad C\to\widehat C\ \ \text{(Yoneda)}
Pseudo-topoi reduced to topoi by passing to a higher universe.
Morphisms of sites; continuous functors
$C$, $C'$ sites, $f\colon C\to C'$ is continuous if the inverse image of a sheaf on $C'$ is a sheaf on $C$:
F\in\widetilde{C'}\ \Longrightarrow\ F\circ f\in\widetilde{C}
Depends only on $\varepsilon_{C'}\circ f\colon C\to\widetilde{C'}$ ($\varepsilon$: object $\mapsto$ its associated sheaf).
\varepsilon_{C'}\circ f\ \simeq\ \tilde f\circ\varepsilon_C,\qquad \tilde f\colon\widetilde C\to\widetilde{C'}\ \text{commuting with arbitrary direct limits}
\operatorname{Hom}_{\varinjlim}(\widetilde C,\widetilde{C'})\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \operatorname{Cont}(C,\widetilde{C'})
Continuous functors depend on neither site.
Criterion for continuity
If $C$, $C'$ have finite inverse limits and $f$ commutes with them: $f$ continuous iff it takes covering families to covering families.
Standard case: open sets of $X'$ and $X$; $g\colon X'\to X$ continuous, $U\mapsto g^{-1}U$.
General case: $X\in C$, $R$ the sieve generated by a covering family $(X_i)$; $C/R$ the objects over $X$ factoring through some $X_i$.
\varepsilon(X)=\varinjlim_{Y\in C/R}\varepsilon(Y)\qquad(\text{characterises covering families})
f\ \text{continuous}\iff \varepsilon_{C'}f(X)=\varinjlim_{Y\in C/R}\varepsilon_{C'}f(Y)
Every colimit-preserving functor between topoi arises so: take small generating subcategories $C$, $C'$ (enlarge $C'$ by the image of $C$).
Morphisms of sites
$\tilde f$ left exact $\Rightarrow$ morphism of topoi.
If $C$, $C'$ have finite inverse limits and the topology of $C'$ is coarser than the canonical one ($C'\to\widetilde{C'}$ fully faithful):
f\ \text{defines a morphism}\ \widetilde C\to\widetilde{C'}\iff f\ \text{continuous and left exact}
Such an $f$ is a morphism of sites (sometimes said from $C'$ to $C$, to match the geometric direction).
Morphisms of a topos $E'$ into $\widetilde C$: functors $\widetilde C\to E'$ commuting with direct limits and finite inverse limits.
C\ \text{stable under finite inverse limits:}\quad \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{top}}(E',\widetilde C)\simeq\{f\colon C\to E'\ \text{left exact, sending covering families to covering families}\}
Geometric meaning independent of the site chosen for the topos.
Morphisms into $\widehat C$
$\widehat C=\widetilde C$ for the coarsest topology: all presheaves are sheaves; covering families are those with a section.
\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{top}}(E,\widehat C)\ \simeq\ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathrm{lex}}(C,E)\qquad(C\ \text{with finite inverse limits})
Continuity empty: families with sections go to families with sections.
So $\widehat C$ classifies functors from $C$ commuting with finite inverse limits.
